Analyst Moretti is left behind in the Vatican, there to play cards with the cardinals and arrange the aforementioned volleyball tournament. [INPUT ARTICLE]Local authority support worker Kinga Michna-Holme was looking for increased professional status and an opportunity for fresh academic challenges when she heard about the Step up to Social Work initiative.
The national scheme offers high-calibre graduates with experience of working with children and families an employment-based and fast-track route to a social work qualification. Last September, Michna-Holme beat off competition from around 2,000 applicants to become one of the first of 192 trainees who have been taken on by 42 different local authorities in England.
Now halfway through the 18-month scheme, Michna-Holme, 35, is employed by Suffolk county council on an annual £15,000 salary. "It's been a fantastic opportunity but it's very hard work as you are working and studying at the same time. You have to be very determined and motivated and well organised," she says. "But the rewards are there. As it's a quicker route to qualification, you are financially supported and you end up with a masters degree."
Applications for the second Step up to Social Work cohort took place last month. Training begins next February and around 214 places are on offer from 53 host local authorities. Candidates must have a minimum 2:1 degree and some experience  either paid or voluntary  of working with children and families. The scheme, funded by the Department for Education, has been created by the Children's Workforce Development Council (CWDC) as a way of helping address the recruitment and retention problems in children and families social work.
While the trainees are qualified to work in either children or adult services, the intention is that they will go on to be employed in childrens' services after they graduate. Keith Brumfitt, CWDC's director for children's trusts, says: "It's something that the employers want, it's something that the candidates want to do and it hits all the right buttons in terms of attracting high quality employees and university entrants to the profession."
The CWDC is optimistic that it will attract the same number of applicants this time round. The rigorous recruitment process is left to the local authorities who, working in regional partnerships, decide how to share out the trainee places. "Local authorities know who they are looking for  it's somebody who is resilient, is committed to the agenda but who also has the soft skills of working with people and the investigative and intellectual skills to look at what he or she is really doing when going out into the field," Brumfitt adds.
Last year 85% of the successful candidates were already employed, working in children and family services either in the public or voluntary sector; others were completing postgraduate study, or came from the private sector but had voluntary experience working with young people. Around half were aged under 30.
The scheme appeals to local authorities because it costs them nothing and trainees learn first hand the culture and day-to-day practices of what they expect from their frontline social workers. For authorities like Suffolk it also means they have another opportunity, outside of the traditional university or grow-your-own sponsored routes, to attract high-achieving graduates.
But there are also other significant spin-offs. Linda James, workforce development manager for children and young people at Suffolk county council, says that for the first time the authority has been able to develop the social work training modules in partnership with the university, which means they can shape the course to reflect their workplace needs. "It's very much been hands on and that is very significant," she says. "From my perspective the employer input is the big boom in the development of the programme."
Brumfitt also believes that initiatives which blend workplace learning with academic study also benefit the wider social worker workforce. "The spin off to existing staff is huge because it creates reflective practice which is quite powerful."

GenAI tools, such as ChatGPT, draw on patterns in language and data to generate anything from essays to videos to mathematical calculations that superficially resemble human work, spurring talk of unprecedented transformation in many fields including academia.
Academics are among those who could face an existential threat if AI is able to replicate - at much faster speeds - research currently done by humans. Many also see the benefits of GenAI's ability to process information and data, which can provide a basis for deeper critical analysis by humans.

CHEATING VERSUS HELPFUL SHORT-CUTS

Some have expressed concern that students might similarly rely on AI to produce work and effectively cheat - especially as AI content gets better with time. Passing off GenAI as original work could also raise copyright issues, prompting questions over whether AI should be banned in academia.

Problems have arisen over what are known as false positives when text written by humans - in some cases by professors trying to test the software - has been flagged as written by AI, though those wrongly accused of using AI can defend themselves if they have saved various drafts of their work.
Students themselves are busy experimenting with AI and some give it a poor grade, saying it can summarise at a basic level, but that facts must always be checked because GenAI cannot distinguish fact from fiction or right from wrong.
Its knowledge is also limited to what it can scrape from the internet, which is not enough for very specific questions.
"I reckon AI has a far way to go before it's properly useful," said Sophie Constant, a 19 year-old law student at England's University of Oxford.
"I can't ask it about a single case. It just doesn't know and it doesn't have access to articles I am studying so it is not very helpful."
CORPORATE SPEED AND SLOW-MOVING REGULATION
UNESCO's latest guidance also flags the risk GenAI will deepen societal divisions as educational and economic success increasingly depend on access to electricity, computers and internet that the poorest do not have.
"We are struggling to align the speed of transformation of the education system to the speed of the change in technological progress," Stefania Giannini, assistant director-general for education at UNESCO, told Reuters.

[INPUT ARTICLE]Many people go into social work because they want to make a difference, however it is important to remember the job can be demanding.
"Social work can be emotionally demanding and it is important that anyone interested in becoming a social worker understands that," says the British Association of Social Workers (BASW).
It is also a sector which has recently been at the centre of media controversy. In 2011, Panorama's account of the abuse of vulnerable young patients at a private hospital near Bristol provoked the government into action.
With so many misconceptions about the sector, what is the reality of working in social care? We spoke to three experts to debunk some of the most popular myths.
Myth 1: social workers are child snatchers
In 2012, the Telegraph reported on UK social workers "snatching" a child from France. It followed the decision by an English court to allow social workers to take a baby from its British parents, even though it was born in France.
Amy Norris, a children's social worker and member of the college of social work, says moving a child from its family to care is the worst part of the job and in reality most work is spent trying to keep children with their families.
"It's the best thing for the children and we want to help people. It's also the law  we have to try and keep children with their families," says Norris.
"So it's not snatching. It's not a quick process," Norris adds. "It might feel quick for the family because it's a difficult process, but there is a lot of thought that's gone into any decisions."
Myth 2: if it's not written down it didn't happen
Maris Stratulis, England manager of BASW, is aware of the importance of keeping records of a child's care, however she believes "the attitude that 'if it's not written down it didn't happen' needs to be challenged".
"How else do you evidence the development of trust that has been created between a social worker and child or vulnerable adult?" Asks Stratulis.
It's more important that the foundation of trust between social worker and child is strong. Stratulis was recently told a story from an adult who was a former child in care and still keeps in contact with her first social worker.
"I don't know how much was recorded in terms of that relationship and the work, but the foundation of trust is still so strong, and that's something that may not be captured within a record," says Stratulis.
Myth 3: there's no career progression
Mark Walford, who founded Trusted Care in 2012, a company which acts as a social care directory, argues against the belief that there is no career progression within the sector.
"I transect the sector and talk to organisations and care workers at the very lowest level, right the way up to the senior managers and owners. There's a lot of people who progress their way up."
Walford's mother has a care agency and all of her staff are grassroots employees. "It's really important to her that that's the case because it gives them a much deeper insight into the sector," he says.
Myth 4: you'll get a low wage
This month, Care UK workers celebrated a pay offer to end their 90 days of strikes. Stratulis thinks that local authorities are finally recognising that there's a competitive climate, offering incentives to retain workers' service. So, things do seem to be moving in the right direction.
Stratulis says: "I am aware of some social workers that would say they're on a reasonable salary. You have to remember though, people don't go into this profession for the money."
Myth 5: residential homes aren't safe for the elderly
A recent ComRes poll found that only 28% of the British public would consider volunteering in a care home, but this number jumped to 76% when those asked were people who had visited a home in the past year.
Walford explains: "The reality is there's a lot of scaremongering across the whole space regarding care homes, a lot of people think they're all terrible."
Trusted Care research in August 2014, however, revealed 88% of user experiences were positive.
Myth 6: A social worker can rush through adoption
Stratulis says the government has made moves to speed up adoption targets, but it's about remembering that this is very complex work.
"It takes the time it does because you've got to make sure you're placing that child in the best possible home," says Stratulis. "And not every child will be suitable for adoption."
Stratulis explains once a recommendation is made, you then have to go through a very lengthy legal process. There's also the whole process of matching.

I like to stick seven or eight to a plain black T-shirt (it gives it a bit of a couture look), but if you'd rather be a little more subtle, then you can go for one or two.
Take-me-anywhere brooches
What you need
Ribbon
Buttons or other embellishments
Needle and thread
Safety pins or brooch pins
Scissors
What to do
Try our step-by-step picture guide if you get confused
1. Choose two different pieces of ribbon in contrasting colours; one should be at least 1cm wider than the other. Cut each piece to an appropriate length: for anything wider than 5cm, half a metre will do; for ribbon about 3-4cm wide, about a third of a metre works well, and for anything thinner, use a quarter of a metre.
2. Using a piece of thread that is about twice at long as the ribbon, sew three stitches over the top of each other at the bottom right of your ribbon. This is the start of your first ruffle and will keep the thread in place.
3. Sew a running stitch all the way along the edge, making sure that each stitch is the same length.
4. Gently pull the thread and push the ribbon down it: this will gather the material and give you the ruffle.
5. Hold the two ends of the ribbon between your thumb and index finger, while still pulling the thread tightly to keep the ruffle, well, ruffled.
6. Oversew the two ends of the ribbon together - this stops the fabric from fraying. Remember to keep the front of the ribbon (usually the shiny side) to the front, and do all your sewing on the back.
7. Make another ruffle with your second piece of ribbon. Sew the smaller one on top of the larger one.
8. Add buttons, beads, sequins, or any other embellishments to the front. Smaller brooches just need one large button, but bigger ones can fit more.
9. Sew a safety pin to the back of the brooch - on the part that doesn't unhinge - and you're finished.

The debate will be in focus on Tuesday when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman makes his first appearance before a Senate panel.

"A video recommendation may not pose as high of a risk as decisions made about health or finances."
Surging popularity of so-called generative AI, which uses data to create new content like ChatGPT's human-sounding prose, has sparked concern the fast-evolving technology could encourage cheating on exams, fuel misinformation and lead to a new generation of scams.

Cave discovery
In 2004, archaeologists first discovered the Blätterhöhle, a long, narrow cave in Hagen, Germany, filled with more than 450 skeletal fragments that belonged to at least 29 individuals. Carbon isotope dating revealed the cave had been used in the Mesolithic period, between 9210 and 8340 B.C., and in the Neolithic period, between 3986 and 2918 B.C. The cool, dry environment provided perfect preservation conditions for the delicate DNA housed within the bones. [See Images of the Excavations]
Bollongino and her colleagues analyzed the fossils' mitochondrial DNA, genetic information carried in the cytoplasm of the cell that is passed on only from the mother, finding usable information in 25 of the individuals.
Separately, the researchers also analyzed carbon and nitrogen isotopes, or variants of the same elements with different molecular weights. Because different foods contain different ratios of heavy and light isotopes, the team was able to pinpoint the diets of the ancient people.

"I think it's very unlikely they did not know of each other or trade, but for some reason, they stayed amongst themselves," Bollongino told LiveScience.

In the second study, researchers analyzed the mitochondrial DNA from more than 364 fossil remains found at more than 20 sites within the Saxony-Anhalt region of Germany, which dated to between 5500 and 1550 B.C.

Thus it is that the world we see, with all its diversity and complexity, is made out of just a handful of elementary particles hopping around according to some simple rules.

Researchers on Friday said they had analyzed the genomes of 23 woolly mammoths - including 16 newly sequenced ones - based on remains preserved in Siberian permafrost. They then compared them to the genomes of 28 modern-day Asian and African elephants.
"The objective was to find those mutations that are present in all mammoths but not in any of the elephants - that is, the genetic adaptations exclusive to the woolly mammoth," said evolutionary geneticist David Díez-del-Molino of the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, lead author of the study published in the journal Current Biology.
"We find that woolly mammoths had molecular adaptations in genes related to coping with cold Arctic environments, such as thick fur, fat storage and metabolism, and thermal sensation, among others," Díez-del-Molino added.
The genomes included a mammoth from 700,000 years ago - near the origination time of this species on the Siberian steppes - and others that lived later in their history, thus showing how genetic adaptations evolved.
The species, which arose at a time when Earth's climate was cooling, inhabited parts of northern Eurasia and North America. Most mammoths went extinct roughly 10,000 years ago amid a warming climate at the last Ice Age's end, with scientists debating whether human hunting played a role. The last ones died out on Wrangel Island off Siberia's coast 4,000 years ago.
The first complete mammoth genome was sequenced in 2015, after a partial genome in 2008.
The new study showed that 92% of unique mutations already existed at the outset of the species, with continued evolution on certain traits. For example, mammoths evolved ever-fluffier fur and ever-smaller ears over time.
"Our 700,000-year-old woolly mammoth may have had larger ears than the mammoths of the last Ice Age," Centre for Palaeogenetics evolutionary geneticist and study senior author Love Dalén said.
One highly evolved gene was one that when "turned off" in laboratory mice results in unusually small ears. Woolly mammoths were about the size of modern African elephants, around 13 feet (4 meters) tall, but had much smaller ears to guard against losing body heat from a larger ear surface.
Several genes involving fur type and growth differed from modern elephants. One of them in humans is associated with Uncombable Hair Syndrome, a condition characterized by dry and frizzy hair that cannot be combed flat. In mammoths, fluffier hair, as well as fat deposits, would have helped provide insulation in the cold.
The mammoths had a mutation in a gene that in people is associated with having dry ear wax, though it is unclear how this gave them any advantage. The same mutation is associated with reduced body odor in the armpits in humans, though this may not mean mammoths had a dainty aroma.
"I very much doubt mammoths would have been sweating into their arm pits. This is a very unique human thing, I think. Other mammals regulate their body temperature in other ways. So it is very unclear if mammoths would have smelled differently because of this gene variant," Dalén said.
The study helped clarify variable shades of mammoth hair color - brownish with a touch of red. Mutations in an immune system-related gene indicated the species adapted to a serious pathogen outbreak at some point.
While the researchers are not involved in trying to resurrect the mammoth through cloning, their work could assist any such effort.
"The dataset we present could be seen as the first element of a road map towards resurrection," Dalén said. "But it should be pointed out that the road ahead is long, likely to be full of pot holes, and in the worst-case scenario leads nowhere."

[INPUT ARTICLE]The oldest human DNA ever recovered is throwing scientists for a loop: The 400,000-year-old genetic material comes from bones that have been linked to Neanderthals in Spain  but its signature is most similar to that of a different ancient human population from Siberia, known as the Denisovans.
The researchers who did the analysis said their findings show an "unexpected link" between two of our extinct cousin species. Follow-up studies could crack the mystery  not only for the early humans who lived in the cave complex known as Sima de los Huesos (Spanish for "Pit of Bones"), but for other mysterious populations in the Pleistocene epoch.
"Ancient DNA sequencing techniques have become sensitive enough to warrant further investigation of DNA survival at sites where Middle Pleistocene hominins are found," the research team, led by Matthias Meyer and Svante Pääbo of Germany's Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, wrote in Thursday's issue of the journal Nature. ("Hominin" is the currently accepted term for humans and our close evolutionary cousins.)
As anthropologists are getting better at extracting DNA from ancient bones, genetic mysteries are cropping up more frequently: Last month, researchers at scientific meetings talked about not-yet-published findings that hinted at interbreeding among Neanderthals, Denisovans and previously unknown populations of early humans.
A new standard
The age of the mitochondrial DNA analyzed for the Nature study sets a new standard: Researchers used statistical analysis of the DNA and other samples to estimate that the material was roughly 400,000 years old. That meshed with the estimated age for similar DNA extracted from bear bones found in the same cave.
More than 6,000 human fossils, representing about 28 individuals, have been recovered from the Sima de los Huesos site, a hard-to-get-to cave chamber that lies about 100 feet (30 meters) below the surface in northern Spain. The fossils are unusually well-preserved, thanks in part to the undisturbed cave's constant cool temperature and high humidity.
The thigh bone of a 400,000-year-old hominin yielded mitochondrial DNA for analysis. Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films
Researchers drilled a series of tiny holes into the cracks in a human femur recovered from the cave to obtain nearly 2 grams (0.07 ounce) of powdered bone. At first, they looked for the signature of ancient nuclear DNA, which could have provided information about the genome of the individual behind the femur  but that information was overwhelmed by the signature of modern-day human contamination.
Then they turned their attention to the mitochondrial DNA, which lies outside the cell's nucleus and is passed down from a mother to her children. That strategy was more successful.
Unusual finding
Previous analysis of bones from the cave had led researchers to assume that the Sima de los Huesos people were closely related to Neanderthals on the basis of their skeletal features. But the mitochondrial DNA was far more similar to that of the Denisovans, an early human population that was thought to have split off from Neanderthals around 640,000 years ago. The first Denisovan specimens were identified in 2010, based on an analysis of 30,000-year-old bones excavated in Siberia.
This skeleton from the Sima de los Huesos cave has been assigned to an early human species known as Homo heidelbergensis. However, researchers say the skeletal structure is similar to that of Neanderthals - so much so that some say the Sima de los Huesos people were actually Neanderthals rather than representatives of Homo heidelbergensis. Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films
The latest DNA analysis sent scientists scrambling for an explanation.
"This unusual finding could be due to at least two different scenarios, both relating to the material inheritance of mtDNA [mitochondrial DNA] and the ease with which it can be lost in a lineage," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at London's Natural History Museum who was not involved in the Nature study, wrote in an email.
One scenario could be that the DNA was passed down the maternal line from a population that was ancestral to the Sima de los Huesos humans as well as the Denisovans, but that the lineage died out among Neanderthals and modern humans.
The other scenario is that an as-yet-undetermined population interbred with ancestors of the Spanish cave-dwellers as well as the Denisovans. Meyer, Pääbo and their colleagues tentatively favor that scenario. "Based on the fossil record, more than one evolutionary lineage may have existed in Europe during the Middle Pleistocene," they write.
"Either way, this new finding can help us start to disentangle the relationships of the various human groups known from the last 600,000 years," Stringer said. "If more mtDNA can be recovered from the Sima 'population' of fossils, it may demonstrate how these individuals were related to each other, and how varied their population was."

That's appropriate, he said, "because I think the real world is messy."
